reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Prior publications have demonstrated associations between gut bacteria and malaria outcomes in Malian and Ugandan children and murine models of malaria have demonstrated differential gut microbiota can cause differential severity of malaria. Murine models also demonstrate gut bacteria compositions change following Plasmodium infection. The present study extends these observations by providing correlations between stool bacteria composition within days of Plasmodium fragile infection in Rhesus macaques, and malaria-naïve US adults infected with Plasmodium falciparum who were participating in a controlled human malaria infection study. In addition to assessment of the pre-infection bacterial composition the present study also assessed post-Plasmodium infection stool bacteria composition at various time points through treatment-induced convalescence. Exciting aspects of this study include the investigation of gut bacteria-induced modulation of malaria in Rhesus macaques as this non-human primate model has the potential to serve as a model to investigate novel gut microbiome-based therapeutics, and the human study which provides the closest assessment of stool bacteria composition prior to Plasmodium infection and its association with malaria outcomes. Stool in the Malian study was collected from children weeks to months before incident Plasmodium infection and in the Ugandan study stool samples were collected from children after hospital admission with severe malaria. Unfortunately, there are a number of weaknesses with the analytical approaches, assumptions, statistical analyses, etc. that raise concerns with the conclusions and substantially dampened enthusiasm for publication of these results.
1. The present analyses do not provide strong evidence in support of the conclusions that have been made.
a. Inclusion of the phrase “High-risk” in the title requires experimental validation to demonstrate causality. At present the analysis only provides an intriguing association. Inclusion of the phrase “high-risk” should be removed throughout the text.
b. Throughout the text the authors refer to “severe parasitemia” or “severe malaria”. I don’t find the data support the use of these desrcriptors. The definition of severe parasitemia in humans is variable in the literature, in lower transmission areas it can be between 2% (100,000 parasites/uL) and 0.5% (25,000 parasites/uL), which might be more relevant for malaria-naive US residents. Based on the authors’ results, peak parasitemia for the severe and mild groups was ~log2 13.5 and ~log11, which is approximately 729 parasites/uL (0.015%) and 60 parasites/uL (0.0012%). Also, it is the highest detected after first passing the threshold (0.250 parasites/uL). Thus, it is hard to say if they would go on to be severe or not, or if there were simply more hours of replication time between infection and PCR detection between the individuals. Within the paper, parasitemia status of humans and macaques were categorically defined based on above and below the average parasitemia at time treatment was initiated. The text should more accurately reflect this by classifying groups as above average parasitemia and below average parasitemia. Additionally, none of the humans or macaques progressed to “severe malaria”, as such this phrase should not be used in the text.
c. In various places in the text (e.g., Line 42, Line 89, etc.) the authors make claims the results “strongly” associate a microbial outcome with malaria outcome. Yet, in many cases the statistical analyses are barely significant. The inclusion of “strong” should be removed in these instances.
2. The authors should provide information on the human subjects (ages, sex, nationality, HbA/S status – if known, etc.). These covariates should be accounted for in the bacterial community analyses. Additionally, the authors should provide a clear description of which subjects received placebo, KAF156 – including dosage, or Malarone. Again, these differential treatments should also be accounted for in stool samples collected post treatment to assess for any treatment induced effects. Finally, the “baseline” stool sample was indicated as being collected -2 to +2 days after infection. Analysis of whether there were differences in when the stool was collected between the severe and mild groups would be helpful to rule out whether that had any impact on microbiome differences.
a. With differential treatments and differential timing of treatments, the study may be better off focusing on association between the pre-infection stool samples and malaria outcomes.
3. Stool samples were reported to be frozen up to 24 hours post collection. As this is a considerable length of time in which bacterial communities can change quite considerably, how much variation in time to -80C is there between subjects and does this explain HC (HC1, HC2, or HC3) status?
4. Bioinformatic analyses
a. The analyses and conclusions would be strengthened by inclusion of multiple alpha diversity metrics.
b. Likewise, the authors should conduct and report on multiple beta diversity metrics.
c. It is not clear that center log ratio (CLR) transformation is the most appropriate. The authors should also report bacteria community analysis on non-transformed read counts.
d. L194: Was differential abundance done on CLR-transformed read counts? It is also not clear if raw read counts were normalized before DESeq2 analysis.
e. Have the authors used appropriate statistical tests for longitudinal analysis?
5. Figure 1
a. Bottom of Panel A indicates Study “Week”, this should be “Day”
b. L212: How many days p.i. for each participant did it take to reach 250 parasites/ml? Are there differences in time to antimalarial treatment between HC1-HC3? Time to treatment (time to peak parasite level) might be related to malaria severity. Did gut microbiota composition affect time to peak parasitemia? When was peak parasitemia reached?
c. Panel C should include CI in the graph.
d. Panel D – would prefer to see this data presented as actual number of parasites/ml rather than non-Log2 transformed. How often was parasitemia measured in the subjects and can the data be presented as area under the parasitemia curve to provide a more cumulative assessment of the parasite burden within each subject over the course of the study? Differences in parasitemia are not that large, and possibly attributable to differences in time between infection and detection. Do the authors have precise time (hours) between infection and parasitemia burden surpassing the treatment threshold? Was parasitemia measured in all individuals at defined time points post infection?
e. Samples were clustered based on gut microbiota composition on CLR transformed data and then investigated for differences in parasitemia, mild (below median) vs severe (above median), and gut bacteria. It would be interesting to analyze based on parasitemia, mild (below median) vs severe (above median) and look for differentially abundant gut bacteria between below average vs above average parasitemia?
f. How do samples cluster based on normalized (non-CLR transformed) read counts data?
g. L218: What is the basis of 3 clusters? Why not two clusters?
h. L230-31: Can it be implied that HC2 enterotype did not impact parasitemia but HC1 and HC3 enterotype modulates parasite burden?
6. Figure S1
a. The data and analyses do not provide strong support that KAF156 or placebo treatment had no effect on bacterial composition. First there is no statistics provided to justify this claim. Second there appears to be differential abundance of the 20 mg KAF156 and 50 mg KAF156 treatment between the HC groups:
i. 20 mg = 60% of HC1 subjects, 15% of HC2 subjects, 56% of HC3 subjects
ii. 50 mg = 20% of HC1 subjects, 54% of HC2 subjects, 22% of HC3 subjects
7. Figure 2
a. A-B ¬– Dimensions 1 and 2 explain only 11% of all variability and there are no statistical analyses of bacterial compositions based on this CLR-transformed PCA plot.
b. L234-37 (A-B): Display this data in a longitudinal fashion using linear mixed effect model for appropriate statistical analysis.
c. C-D – by far the more informative analysis as it focuses on baseline stool samples, but again there are not statistical analyses to go along with these data.
d. Panel E – would be better displayed as the average number of ASVs among subjects within the three HC groups, showing ranges, and statistical analysis.
e. Panel F shows significant difference in Shannon diversity at baseline between HC1 and HC2, yet there are no differences in parasitemia between these groups in Figure 1D.
8. Figure S2
a. Lines 237-239 indicate that Dim3 differentiates bacterial communities between HC1 compared to HC2 and HC3.
i. HC1 symbols are difficult to see.
ii. There are only 6 stool samples that appear to differentiate on Dim3 from the rest of the samples. This doesn’t lend strong support the claims made in Lines 234-243.
iii. These data would be more informative if they were the baseline samples.
9. Line 233 refers to malaria “progression”. It is not clear what is meant, and since all subjects developed patent parasitemia followed by treatment, this statement should probably be removed.
10. L260: There are no data regarding transient changes induced by P. falciparum infection.
11. Figure 3
a. Figure 3 and Figure 6 – It would be nice to see compositional data. What percentage of the microbiome is represented by the taxa. It is just the prevalence (presence/absence) within a cluster and CLR counts, which are standardized by each taxa, so you can’t tell how prevalent the bacteria are. The differences between the taxa in the severe and mild group could be very minimal, but statistically significant.
b. Panel B is missing label on Y-axis and would be more appropriate to only include those taxonomy that are significant following Bonferroni correction.
c. Panel B: Do linear mixed effect modeling unless data are solely baseline data.
d. L280: What is meant by this sentence? There are no apparent data provided to support this claim.
e. Panel D-H – what criteria were used to selection of “select differentially abundant genera”. What statistical test was used?
f. Panel I – Are any of these taxa showing significant differences between time points (statistics)? Do they behave differently between the groups?
12. Figure 4
a. Again “mild” and “severe” parasitemia are not defined. Based on the human study, this is presumably categorically defined as parasitemia below or above average, respectively.
b. The Y axis in 4C is labelled as % parasitemia, but the legend lists it as being log2-transformed. I think it is probably untransformed parasitemia, as otherwise it would be much lower than the human parasitemia (which doesn’t make sense given the different treatment thresholds), also Fig S4 uses untransformed parasitemia.
c. Panel B: Is divisive hierarchical clustering based on CLR transformed data?
13. Figure 5
a. Analysis would be much stronger if focused on the Week 0 stool sample. Indeed, data in panel C suggest there are little to no differences between the groups, which questions interpretation of data presented in Figure 4.
b. The authors need to provide statistical analyses of these comparisons
c. What is “microbiome bins”?
d. L322: Data is not interpretable unless shown in longitudinal fashion. Distance of each time point can be calculated from the baseline and plotted to see the impact of infection on gut microbiota.
14. Figure S3
a. Analysis of the Week 0 sample reveals no difference. This outcome, combined with the lack of statistical analysis and near overlapping samples in the Week 0 UniFrac distance PCoA plot (Figure 5C) argues against the conclusion provided in Lines 322-324.
15. Figure S4
a. Provision of parasitemia curves with all time points would be optimal. Additionally, those data should then be analyzed as area under the parasitemia curve to assess cumulative parasite burden over time within each macaque. This would provide additional information to that provided in Figure 4.
b. Line 315 – What is community organization?
c. Line 323 – “variable levels of microbiota” makes it sound like different quantities of microbiota
16. Figure 6
a. Panel B is missing label on Y-axis and would be more appropriate to only include those taxonomy that are significant following Bonferroni correction.
17. The authors need to acknowledge of some of the possible limitations of the study. The gut microbiota is known to be different between Western and non-industrialized societies, so the microbiota composition associated with protection here might not be the same as those associated with protection in Africa. Also, malaria interventions, like vaccination, have a history of working very well in healthy US adults but then not being transferrable to African children in malaria endemic areas, possibly microbiota related, but maybe also due to previous exposure to malaria (and other pathogens), overall health and nutrition, etc.
Additional comments:
1. For accuracy, it would be optimal for the authors to use the descriptor “healthy US adults” throughout the study in place of “humans” to avoid inference to African children, or other tropical regions, that suffer from the vast majority of P. falciparum infections.
2. L184: Taxonomic assignment was performed using old gg database. The authors should confirm the fundamental findings using updated SILVA database.
3. L198: The authors should deposit custom scripts and codes to GitHub page.
4. Line 207: age range of the US adults should be included.
5. L266: ASVs instead of ASCs.
6. Multiple occasions within the Results the authors make note of non-significant differences. These comments should be excluded or limited as there is no strong justification to discuss those things that are not different.
7. The authors may want to consider going from the macaque study to the human study. It felt awkward going from the gold-standard human malaria study to the macaque “model organism” study.
8. Regarding the author’s claim that the RM model is a good translational model, Bifidobacterium is seen in their human data set as a taxon of interest and noted that previous studies have also seen this, but this was not observed in the RM.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper examines the microbiome of (1) humans who are challenged with P. falciapurum malaria by infected mosquito bite and (2) NHP who are challenged with P.fragile malaria by injection of infected red blood cells. Both the humans and the NHP were subdivided into two groups, “high parasitemia” and “low parasitemia”. There were microbiome differences between the two groups that were identified with unsupervised clustering. My main concerns with this article are with the clinical definitions and descriptions of the CHMI.
Human CHMI:
- The human CHMI was conducted as part of an antimalarial drug study (KAF156). The current paper evaluates microbiomes from 35 participants in that study, from the placebo group, the 20 mg group, and the 50 mg group (lines 103-104. Of note, in looking at the original publication of KAF157, 3 of the volunteers in the 50 mg group did not get malaria. Therefore, their inclusion in this study is questionable.
- The participants were divided into two groups of “mild” or “severe” parasitemia (lines 218-219) based on whether their parasitemia was above or below a median parasitemia value. This is an extremely flawed way to differentiate the participants clinically. All of the participants were diagnosed with a highly sensitive molecular test. Based on the parent study, few had malaria symptoms, and none had severe malaria (if the clinical study site had allowed severe malaria to occur in the context of a drug efficacy study, this would be unethical). All mention of “severe malaria” and “severe parasitemia” needs to be removed from the manuscript if it is considered for publication. In addition, although the parasitemia levels are quantitative, the timing of sample collection in relation to the exact time of the CHMI and the exact time within the synchronized cycles of parasite emergence from RBC all affect the parasitemia levels. High parasitemia levels in the setting of ongoing malaria infection correlate with malaria severity. Differences between very low levels that are detected soon after blood stage infection has started also reflect some amount of luck (what time was the CHMI 8 days ago? What time was the volunteers appointment on the day of the PCR blood draw). This makes dividing a grouping of 35 very low parasitemias, 3 of which had a value of “ZERO” into two groups questionable.
- Nonetheless, the authors have found differences between the two groups (figure 1B) that may be worth considering. However, the statistics that differentiate the two groups of parasitemia within the three clusters (lines 220-228) are not described and need to be specified. Also, it would be helpful to know the actual parasitemia levels that were being discussed (which presumably were very low).
- Consider a discussion of the fact that most of the malaria infection was a liver infection. The blood stage of infection was brief before treatment was initiated – how does this relate to your postulations about the authors’ observations of the microbiome?
NHP challenge:
- The authors state that this is a new challenge model and provide a rationale for why this challenge model is suitable for microbiome/malaria studies. As a new model, many important details were lacking:
o What clinical manifestations were observed in the animals, and what parasitemia levels were these clinical manifestations associated with? Line 300 states that P.fragile induces similar clinical signs in RM as in Pf in humans – does this include cerebral malaria and other clinical manifestations of severe malaria? Also, which/how many of the animals needed the escalated treatment regimens, and which did not?
o Treatment regimen questions: Why did the treatment begin only after parasitema was >0.5% and not as soon as parasitemia was detectable? The treatment regimens appeared to be titrated to be lower than abortive – there was an expectation that one regimen could be given for 2 weeks consecutively without clearing parasitemia. If sub-abortive treatment was being used, why?
o How was “high parasite load” defined (line 304)? (defined for the humans but I did not see it for the RM.
o Line 349 “more severe P. fragile infection” – without information about clinical symptoms in this new animal model, I don’t know how to assess this (whereas in humans there were NO severe P. falciparum infections)
Relating the human challenge to the NHP challenge: Human challenge was by infected mosquito bite, therefore, there was 7 days of clinically silent liver infection prior to blood stage infection, which was treated at a very early stage (because it was detected molecularly, which is a very sensitive method of detection. NHP challenge was by injection of infected RBC, so there is no liver stage infection. NHP challenge seemed to be permissive of ongoing parasitemia, and it is unknown what symptoms the NHP had. The many differences between the human challenge and the NHP challenge, and whether the data are comparable to each other in consideration of all these differences need to be discussed.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This is an interesting study but there are a few areas that require further clarification, and the overall conclusion is not clearly demonstrated by the results and figures as they currently are presented.
Abstract
- How similar is P. fragile to P. falciparum? Since these are being directly compared, the authors should explicitly compare how similar or different these two infections are
- Some statements seem over-stated, like “the combined weight of this evidence demonstrates that pre-infection GI microbiome composition is highly indicative of P. falciparum disease risk” (but yet the combined data is not on P. falciparum, half of it is on P. fragile)
Materials and Methods
- This is a nice sized human study (35 people) paired with a nice sized macaque study (16)
- Stool samples are collected in such a way that it is unclear whether there was enough time for any microbes to replicate during the time period between collection and storage (“within 24hours of collection”). A major suggestion here is that the authors need to do an analysis of time interval between collection and freezing and the results (if there is indeed an impact of time interval between collection and freezing, this would undermine the results and suggest that some of the collections were not frozen down quick enough to get a good sense of the microbial community)
- The stool collection for the macaques is well done and thought-out with respect to collecting stool from individual animals and immediately storing it at -80C
- Why do the authors use the 357F-806R primers (those published and used originally by the Earth Microbiome Project)? These are not necessarily the best primers for studies related to human gut microbiome health. I think other options should have been considered, or at least the authors should consider whether they are missing any information that they could have gained by using a different set of primers.
Results
- The authors should clarify whether the HC1 group could have another issue that confounds the data (e.g. low yield). The authors should show an analysis in which they see whether any metadata affect the groupings (e.g., total DNA yield, time between collection and freezing, etc)
- Similarly, in the rhesus macaque study, the authors should also test and consider whether there is a cage/room effect. Even though the authors do a great job of making sure they are collecting the stool from a specific animal, this doesn’t rule out the very likely possibility that socially housed animals may have more similar microbiomes than those in which they are not housed. The authors should do a analysis with metadata to see whether any of their clustering patterns are associated with these logistical factors (e.g., cage, room)
- In Line 323, I am unclear on how the authors conclude that “parasite burden was primarily driven by major compositional differences, rather than variable levels of microbiota found in both groups”. This point should be further explained. Particularly the idea that parasite burden itself is “driven” by microbiome differences. I did not find evidence in this paper that parasite burden is definitively “driven” by microbiome differences.
Discussion
- The authors seem to interchange the concepts of parasitemia, “disease progression”, etc and it is unclear what the main message is that they are trying to say – are they arguing that gut microbiota composition CAUSES parasitemia to be higher or lower? Or is this a mere association without a known causation. The wording here should be clarified.
- The overall idea seems to be that pre-infection microbiome composition can predict the severity of the malaria infection. Could the authors create a model to test this theory (by using part of their data and doing cross-validation to see if this holds up?)
- Going back to the main conclusion of the paper, the authors state that they “identified a high-risk microbial signature that is strongly associated with increased risk of developing severe parasitemia” and they say they find this in both humans and rhesus macaques, but after reading the paper and looking at the figures, I still am not clear on what exact microbes are associated with this increased risk of severe disease (that are in common between humans and rhesus macaques).

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-by-point response to the reviewers
We thank the editors and the reviewers for their helpful and thoughtful feedback on our manuscript that has the updated title of “Distinct gastrointestinal microbial signatures predict acute parasite levels in controlled Plasmodium infections in both rhesus macaques and humans”. We have addressed the issues brought up by the reviewers (detailed below) and believe our manuscript is greatly improved. Thank you for your time and consideration of our manuscript.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Prior publications have demonstrated associations between gut bacteria and malaria outcomes in Malian and Ugandan children and murine models of malaria have demonstrated differential gut microbiota can cause differential severity of malaria. Murine models also demonstrate gut bacteria compositions change following Plasmodium infection. The present study extends these observations by providing correlations between stool bacteria composition within days of Plasmodium fragile infection in Rhesus macaques, and malaria-naïve US adults infected with Plasmodium falciparum who were participating in a controlled human malaria infection study. In addition to assessment of the pre-infection bacterial composition the present study also assessed post-Plasmodium infection stool bacteria composition at various time points through treatment-induced convalescence. Exciting aspects of this study include the investigation of gut bacteria-induced modulation of malaria in Rhesus macaques as this non-human primate model has the potential to serve as a model to investigate novel gut microbiome-based therapeutics, and the human study which provides the closest assessment of stool bacteria composition prior to Plasmodium infection and its association with malaria outcomes. Stool in the Malian study was collected from children weeks to months before incident Plasmodium infection and in the Ugandan study stool samples were collected from children after hospital admission with severe malaria. Unfortunately, there are a number of weaknesses with the analytical approaches, assumptions, statistical analyses, etc. that raise concerns with the conclusions and substantially dampened enthusiasm for publication of these results.
We thank the reviewer for their positive comments regarding our investigation of gut bacteria-induced modulation of malaria in Rhesus macaques and assessment of stool bacteria composition in humans during malaria infection. We also thank the reviewer for their detailed and thoughtful questions and comments on each component of our manuscript. We have detailed our specific efforts to address these points and improve the manuscript in our responses below.
1. The present analyses do not provide strong evidence in support of the conclusions that have been made.
a. Inclusion of the phrase “High-risk” in the title requires experimental validation to demonstrate causality. At present the analysis only provides an intriguing association. Inclusion of the phrase “high-risk” should be removed throughout the text.
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We have removed the phrase “high-risk” from the title and have changed it to be “Distinct gastrointestinal microbial signatures predict acute parasite levels in controlled Plasmodium infections in both rhesus macaques and humans” (Page 1, Line 1). We have also removed the phrase “high-risk” from the abstract and throughout the manuscript (Page 2, Line 51).
b. Throughout the text the authors refer to “severe parasitemia” or “severe malaria”. I don’t find the data support the use of these desrcriptors. The definition of severe parasitemia in humans is variable in the literature, in lower transmission areas it can be between 2% (100,000 parasites/uL) and 0.5% (25,000 parasites/uL), which might be more relevant for malaria-naive US residents. Based on the authors’ results, peak parasitemia for the severe and mild groups was ~log2 13.5 and ~log11, which is approximately 729 parasites/uL (0.015%) and 60 parasites/uL (0.0012%). Also, it is the highest detected after first passing the threshold (0.250 parasites/uL). Thus, it is hard to say if they would go on to be severe or not, or if there were simply more hours of replication time between infection and PCR detection between the individuals. Within the paper, parasitemia status of humans and macaques were categorically defined based on above and below the average parasitemia at time treatment was initiated. The text should more accurately reflect this by classifying groups as above average parasitemia and below average parasitemia. Additionally, none of the humans or macaques progressed to “severe malaria”, as such this phrase should not be used in the text.
We agree with the reviewer that our use of the phrases “severe malaria” and “severe parasitemia” did not accurately reflect the parasitemia categories that we used in our analyses. To avoid confusion, we have therefore edited the manuscript to refer only to “parasitemia” and to describe groups as “above median parasitemia” and “below median parasitemia” where appropriate, as recommended by the reviewer.
c. In various places in the text (e.g., Line 42, Line 89, etc.) the authors make claims the results “strongly” associate a microbial outcome with malaria outcome. Yet, in many cases the statistical analyses are barely significant. The inclusion of “strong” should be removed in these instances.
We have removed the word “strong” from the manuscript text (Page 2, Line 52; Page 3, Line 60; Page 5, Line 113; Page 21, Line 573; Page 24, Line 664; Page 28, Line 757; Page 31, Line 854).
2. The authors should provide information on the human subjects (ages, sex, nationality, HbA/S status – if known, etc.). These covariates should be accounted for in the bacterial community analyses. Additionally, the authors should provide a clear description of which subjects received placebo, KAF156 – including dosage, or Malarone. Again, these differential treatments should also be accounted for in stool samples collected post treatment to assess for any treatment induced effects. Finally, the “baseline” stool sample was indicated as being collected -2 to +2 days after infection. Analysis of whether there were differences in when the stool was collected between the severe and mild groups would be helpful to rule out whether that had any impact on microbiome differences.
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Data on age and sex for the CHMI participants were published in the original KAF156 study (PMID: 32644127). Data on nationality and HbA/S status are unfortunately not available. For sex, with the exception of 1 female in the 50mg post-exposure KAF156 group, all study participants were male, thus, we do not account for sex in our analyses. We have, however, now included Supplementary Figures 6A and B that depict analyses we conducted to assess whether participant age or BMI were different across clusters. We found that there were no significant differences in either age or BMI between CHMI participants stratified into either HC1, HC2, or HC3. We have incorporated these findings into the manuscript text (Page 17, Lines 472-473).
For treatments, all CHMI participants were treated with Malarone prior to collection of the final follow-up sample. We have now clarified this in the methods section (Page 7, Lines 191-192). We have now also included Supplementary Figure 6C, which depicts the number of CHMI participants in each cluster that received either placebo or 20mg or 50mg KAF156 post-CHMI. We evaluated the distribution of treatment modalities across clusters via Fisher’s exact test and found that the differences between groups were not significant (p=0.195). We have incorporated these findings in the manuscript (Pages 17-18, Lines 473-477).
Given that no significant differences were found between the distribution of treatment groups across the clusters, we are confident that the post-inoculation KAF156 treatment did not impact our results, particularly as we have focused our associations of parasitemia with pre-infection microbiome data, as recommended by Reviewer 1 in Point 2a (see below).
In terms of analysis of whether there were differences in when stool was collected between the above and below median parasitemia groups, we reviewed what day stool was collected from each participant relative to P. falciparum inoculation. We found that of the n=32 participants included in our analysis, n=2 participants had stool collected 2 days prior to CHMI (day -2), n=15 participants had stool collected 1 day prior to CHMI (day -1), n=12 participants had stool collected the day of CHMI (day 0), and n=3 participants had stool collected 1 day after CHMI (day 1). None of the 3 participants that had stool collected after CHMI were in HC1, which was the group that had greater risk of above median parasitemia. Of the two participants that had stool collected two days prior to CHMI, one was in HC1 and the other was in HC2. From these data, we can conclude that the collection date did not have a consistent relationship with microbiome profile.
a. With differential treatments and differential timing of treatments, the study may be better off focusing on association between the pre-infection stool samples and malaria outcomes.
We agree with the reviewer that focusing on the associations between the pre-infection stool samples and malaria outcomes is preferred. Indeed, while we included some analyses in the paper which examine microbial community changes following challenge (alpha diversity, core microbiome), the microbiome-based clustering we use to assess risk is based on aggregated pre-inoculation data for the RMs or pre-challenge data from the CHMI participants. We have made efforts throughout the manuscript to clarify when the aggregated pre-treatment data is being assessed.
3. Stool samples were reported to be frozen up to 24 hours post collection. As this is a considerable length of time in which bacterial communities can change quite considerably, how much variation in time to -80C is there between subjects and does this explain HC (HC1, HC2, or HC3) status?
We agree with the reviewer that immediate freezing of the human CHMI samples would have been ideal. Unfortunately, although we ensured that all samples were frozen within 24hours of collection, data on the exact amount of time that each sample was kept at room temperature prior to freezing was not collected, thus we are unable to conduct any analyses to see whether length of time prior to freezing was associated with differences between the three CHMI groups. We are, however, reassured that room temperature storage of stool samples of less than 24hours would likely not impact our conclusions based on prior studies of lengthy room temperature storage of fecal specimens. Indeed, prior work has shown that storage of stool samples for 72hours at room temperature has been reported to cause less shifts in detected communities than chemical storage methods (PMID: 26572876). An even lengthier preservation of 1 week at room temperature as compared to immediate freezing demonstrated that variation within donors was less than variation between samples frozen immediate or kept at room temperature for 1 week (PMID: 27822526). We have incorporated these references and this limitation into the discussion of our manuscript (Page 30, Lines 814-824).
4. Bioinformatic analyses.
a. The analyses and conclusions would be strengthened by inclusion of multiple alpha diversity metrics.
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment and now include in the manuscript additional measures of alpha diversity that address the compositional makeup of individual samples in three ways: 1) we address Shannon diversity, which is a commonly used approach; 2) we provide richness data that is evaluated in the context of sequencing depth; and 3) we provide information on the core microbiome, specifically what percent of the total sample is comprised of core microbes.
b. Likewise, the authors should conduct and report on multiple beta diversity metrics.
Because 16s rRNA studies are compositional in nature, we utilized a compositionally aware method of normalizing count data (see response to point 4C below for greater detail/references). Using the CLR to account for differences in sequencing depth means that assessing differences between samples (beta diversity) should be done using Aitchison distance, which is the Euclidean distance between samples that have been normalized using CLR.
c. It is not clear that center log ratio (CLR) transformation is the most appropriate. The authors should also report bacteria community analysis on non-transformed read counts.
Normalizing 16s rRNA and other sequencing data types remains an active area of investigation. The relative nature of the data (compositionality) means that a reduced detection of a given taxa in relative terms could be due to a true decrease in the sample, or that levels remain the same but appear lower due to an increase in another taxa. CLR and other compositionally aware methods that address this “sum of 1” constraint by creating ratios instead of proportions. While we provide raw read counts within the paper, it would be inappropriate to assess non-transformed raw read counts due to differences in sequencing depth.
d. L194: Was differential abundance done on CLR-transformed read counts? It is also not clear if raw read counts were normalized before DESeq2 analysis.
As stated in the methods section (Page 9, Lines 235-237), raw read counts were used for DESeq2 analysis, which is essential to satisfy assumptions of this analysis.
e. Have the authors used appropriate statistical tests for longitudinal analysis?
The reviewer raises an important question for microbiome analyses using sequential sampling from the same individuals. Mixed effects models that account for the nested correlations within individuals are useful tools for addressing these constrains. In this study, however, we do not make comparisons over time where individuals have multiple datapoints. Because we found evidence that baseline microbiome composition predicted risk for parasitemia following Plasmodium exposure, we did not perform differential abundance assessments of changes in microbiome composition induced by infection. Therefore, these models were not employed here.
5. Figure 1
a. Bottom of Panel A indicates Study “Week”, this should be “Day”
We have removed the study timeline from this figure. Please note, as per Reviewer 1’s suggestion to discuss the RM results first followed by the CHMI results, Figure 1 is now Figure 5.
b. L212: How many days p.i. for each participant did it take to reach 250 parasites/ml? Are there differences in time to antimalarial treatment between HC1-HC3? Time to treatment (time to peak parasite level) might be related to malaria severity. Did gut microbiota composition affect time to peak parasitemia? When was peak parasitemia reached?
The reviewer raises a good point. In fact, the days p.i. to reach 250 parasites/ml was variable and related to the post-infection KAF treatment, which was outlined in the original manuscript (PMID: 32644127). However, the microbiome clusters we identified (HC1, HC2, and HC3) were determined by pre-infection, pre-treatment microbiome composition, and assessment of treatment distribution showed that there were no significant differences in treatment assignment between clusters HC1, HC2, and HC3. This finding is now demonstrated in Supplemental Figure S6. Beyond statistics, HC1 and HC3, which evidenced the greatest difference in risk for elevated parasitemia, are virtually identical in their treatment assignments (Fig. S6C) and were equally influenced by post-infection treatment.
c. Panel C should include CI in the graph.
The updated Figure 5C (Formerly Figure 1) now includes confidence intervals.
d. Panel D – would prefer to see this data presented as actual number of parasites/ml rather than non-Log2 transformed. How often was parasitemia measured in the subjects and can the data be presented as area under the parasitemia curve to provide a more cumulative assessment of the parasite burden within each subject over the course of the study? Differences in parasitemia are not that large, and possibly attributable to differences in time between infection and detection. Do the authors have precise time (hours) between infection and parasitemia burden surpassing the treatment threshold? Was parasitemia measured in all individuals at defined time points post infection?
To enhance our ability to compare changes in parasitemia between CHMI participants and RM models, parasite burden for both studies now include a z-score of parasitemia. We also include the direct parasitemia results collected by the distinct measurement methods. Therefore, for RMs (Figure 1B), we depict z-score for % infected RBC (black lines, left axis), as well as the actual % infected RBC (red lines, right axis). For humans (Figure 5B), we depict z-score for parasites/ml (black lines), as well as the actual parasites/ml (red lines), no longer in log2 format, which was originally used to aid visual interpretation but may have impeded easy interpretation of parasite levels.
As outlined in the original KAF156 study (PMID: 32644127), parasitemia in CHMI participants was measured daily until subjects reached treatment criteria, at which time treatment began. CHMI participants were then assessed until parasite burden dropped and remained below treatment levels. Unfortunately, records from the original study do not include the precise time in hours and minutes that elapsed between infection and parasitemia.
Importantly, we utilize the pairwise Wilcoxon tests here, which evaluate by rank and not exact parasite levels. The use of a non-parametric test is important in clinical data when the assumption of normality required by T tests is not assumed. Additionally, T tests are sensitive to outliers, where the Wilcoxon tests is not.
e. Samples were clustered based on gut microbiota composition on CLR transformed data and then investigated for differences in parasitemia, mild (below median) vs severe (above median), and gut bacteria. It would be interesting to analyze based on parasitemia, mild (below median) vs severe (above median) and look for differentially abundant gut bacteria between below average vs above average parasitemia?
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. We conducted differential abundance analysis with participants segregated into either above or below median peak peripheral parasitemia, but this approach only yielded one ASV, an unresolved Catenibacterium, that associated with increased peripheral parasitemia (Pages 21-22, Lines 585-588, Supplemental Figure S8B). To overcome this limitation, we employed a multivariate method known as partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) which has greater power to resolve differences between groups and combines information from microbiome clustering and parasite levels. This technique allowed us to confirm the important distinctions across hierarchically determined clusters made by differential abundance analysis, while also prioritizing taxa that most discriminate between groups. Our use of this approach includes a combined score that was generated from independent assessments of microbiome cluster and parasite burden. This allows us to investigate the most defining taxa between above median and below median parasitemia in the context of original clusters (Page 22-23, Lines 600-625).
f. How do samples cluster based on normalized (non-CLR transformed) read counts data?
It would not be appropriate to cluster without transformation, as the major discriminator would become sequencing depth, not composition.
g. L218: What is the basis of 3 clusters? Why not two clusters?
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. Cluster assignments can be subjective and require some interpretation from the analyst. Considering the new Figure 5C (originally Figure 1B), the divisive tree can be interpreted from the top down. Using this approach, we see that the first three splits (horizontal lines) separate what we call HC1 from the rest of the baseline samples, indicating they are the most “different”. The fourth major horizontal split separates 2 sample groups, which we call HC2 and HC3. This approach creates interpretable splits and, by change, 3 balanced groups in terms of size. While one could argue that HC2 and HC3 could be combined, this would ignore the fact that they are cleanly split, and that HC2 has greater vertical line heights, indicating more variability within this cluster than HC1. This interpretation is reinforced by examining the PCoA plot shown in Figure 6A.
h. L230-31: Can it be implied that HC2 enterotype did not impact parasitemia but HC1 and HC3 enterotype modulates parasite burden?
Using Figure 5C, we see that CHMI participants in HC2 had an estimated 4-fold increase in the likelihood of being in the above median parasitemia group as compared to participants grouped in HC3. While these results are not statistically significant (p=0.149), when combined with the data shown in Figure 5B, where HC2 has elevated parasitemia compared to HC3, it suggests some underlying biology. It is possible that future cohorts with a larger sample size would move these results from trends to significance.
6. Figure S1
a. The data and analyses do not provide strong support that KAF156 or placebo treatment had no effect on bacterial composition. First there is no statistics provided to justify this claim. Second there appears to be differential abundance of the 20 mg KAF156 and 50 mg KAF156 treatment between the HC groups:
i. 20 mg = 60% of HC1 subjects, 15% of HC2 subjects, 56% of HC3 subjects
ii. 50 mg = 20% of HC1 subjects, 54% of HC2 subjects, 22% of HC3 subjects
We agree with the reviewer that a statistical assessment is useful here. To assess if the treatments were significantly associated with the microbiome clusters, we first created a contingency table that summarized the number of samples from each treatment with each cluster. Because several cells in the contingency table had small counts (less than 5), we used Fisher’s Exact Test instead of the chi-squared test. Supplemental Figure S6 provides the proportions of treatments within each cluster and reveals an insignificant difference in treatment assignment. More simply, the contingency table shows that the number of individuals assigned to each treatment from HC1 and HC3, where the greatest difference in peak parasitemia occurred, are virtually identical:
To address the math provided by the reviewer, this works out to 60% of HC1 subjects and 56% of HC3 subjects receiving the KAF156 treatment at the 20mg dose, 20% of HC1 subjects and 22% of HC3 subjects receiving the KAV156 treatment at the 50mg dose, and 20% of HC1 subjects and 22% of HC3 subjects receiving placebo.
7. Figure 2
a. A-B – Dimensions 1 and 2 explain only 11% of all variability and there are no statistical analyses of bacterial compositions based on this CLR-transformed PCA plot.
In our new Figure 6A, the amount of variability explained by the first two principal components amounts to 14%. While this is an increase over 11%, we would not argue that this is “better”. The amount of variability explained by two components of PCoA (or dimensions of PCA) is always related to the sample population. For example, if we examined a population that included strict vegans and enthusiastic meat eaters, we would likely see far more variability. Here, the patient population was selected for its similarity in terms of age and overall health, and due to volunteer rates, were predominantly male. Thus the 14% suggests that while we find significant differences between groups in each of the first two components (see new Supplemental Figure S7A), their microbiomes contain a high degree of overlap, which would be expected in this case. Thus, our downstream analysis focuses on the differences that do exist within this population. We also now include statistical evaluation of the distances traveled by each subject over time (Supplemental Figure 6A).
b. L234-37 (A-B): Display this data in a longitudinal fashion using linear mixed effect model for appropriate statistical analysis.
We are unclear on what the Reviewer means by showing the PCA in longitudinal fashion. However, our new PCoA plots highlight baseline and final samples, and connect samples within an individual over time to track variability over time within each group (Figure 2A and Figure 6A).
c. C-D – by far the more informative analysis as it focuses on baseline stool samples, but again there are not statistical analyses to go along with these data.
We thank the Reviewer for this comment and believe that this is addressed by our response to Points 7A and B above.
d. Panel E – would be better displayed as the average number of ASVs among subjects within the three HC groups, showing ranges, and statistical analysis.
We appreciate this comment from the Reviewer. Our analysis of sequencing depth now shows a range of sequencing depths in each microbiome cluster (Supplemental Figure S7C), and also shows that baseline differences in observed ASVs (richness) was not impacted by sequencing depth (Supplemental Figure S7D).
e. Panel F shows significant difference in Shannon diversity at baseline between HC1 and HC2, yet there are no differences in parasitemia between these groups in Figure 1D.
We agree with the reviewer that significant differences do exist in Shannon diversity and although parasitemia is elevated in HC1 compared to HC2, this difference does not reach statistical significance (p=0.17, Figure 5B), possibly due to our small sample size. To clarify, we do not propose in our analysis that alpha diversity itself is the sole driver of differences in parasitemia. Rather, our data suggests that the increased diversity in HC1 is at the expense of a decreased core microbiome, and that the taxa missing or reduced from the core microbiome are the drivers of increased parasitemia. This relationship between loss of core microbiome and increase in parasitemia is reinforced by our regression analysis shown in Figure 6F.
8. Figure S2
a. Lines 237-239 indicate that Dim3 differentiates bacterial communities between HC1 compared to HC2 and HC3.
This figure has been removed from the revised manuscript, but to address the Reviewer’s concern, we note that the 3-dimensional PCA plot in the original manuscript can be difficult to interpret due to constrains in the figure’s development in the R environment. While presenting taxa as a percentage of the sample might intuitively seem more straightforward, microbiome data inherently comes with compositional constraints that can lead to misinterpretation if not properly addressed.
The primary challenge with microbiome data lies in its compositional nature; the data are proportions and sum to a constant (e.g., 100%), which introduces a dependency between taxa. This dependency complicates the direct comparison of raw or percentage abundance data across samples because differences in the abundance of one taxon necessarily affect the apparent abundances of others, due to the constant sum constraint. This issue is known as the “compositionality problem.”
To address this, we employed the Centered Log Ratio (CLR) transformation, which is a widely recognized method for analyzing compositional data. The CLR transformation mitigates the compositional constraint by converting proportions to log-ratios, thus enabling the comparison of relative abundances across samples in a mathematically coherent and interpretable manner. By using CLR-transformed values, we can directly compare the relative dominance and variation of taxa across different conditions (e.g., above and below median parasitemia groups) without the misleading effects that arise from the compositional nature of the data. ### Reviewer 1

Prior publications have demonstrated associations between gut bacteria and malaria outcomes in Malian and Ugandan children and murine models of malaria have demonstrated differential gut microbiota can cause differential severity of malaria. Murine models also demonstrate gut bacteria compositions change following Plasmodium infection. The present study extends these observations by providing correlations between stool bacteria composition within days of Plasmodium fragile infection in Rhesus macaques, and malaria-naïve US adults infected with Plasmodium falciparum who were participating in a controlled human malaria infection study. In addition to assessment of the pre-infection bacterial composition the present study also assessed post-Plasmodium infection stool bacteria composition at various time points through treatment-induced convalescence. Exciting aspects of this study include the investigation of gut bacteria-induced modulation of malaria in Rhesus macaques as this non-human primate model has the potential to serve as a model to investigate novel gut microbiome-based therapeutics, and the human study which provides the closest assessment of stool bacteria composition prior to Plasmodium infection and its association with malaria outcomes. Stool in the Malian study was collected from children weeks to months before incident Plasmodium infection and in the Ugandan study stool samples were collected from children after hospital admission with severe malaria. Unfortunately, there are a number of weaknesses with the analytical approaches, assumptions, statistical analyses, etc. that raise concerns with the conclusions and substantially dampened enthusiasm for publication of these results.
1. The present analyses do not provide strong evidence in support of the conclusions that have been made.
a. Inclusion of the phrase “High-risk” in the title requires experimental validation to demonstrate causality. At present the analysis only provides an intriguing association. Inclusion of the phrase “high-risk” should be removed throughout the text.
b. Throughout the text the authors refer to “severe parasitemia” or “severe malaria”. I don’t find the data support the use of these desrcriptors. The definition of severe parasitemia in humans is variable in the literature, in lower transmission areas it can be between 2% (100,000 parasites/uL) and 0.5% (25,000 parasites/uL), which might be more relevant for malaria-naive US residents. Based on the authors’ results, peak parasitemia for the severe and mild groups was ~log2 13.5 and ~log11, which is approximately 729 parasites/uL (0.015%) and 60 parasites/uL (0.0012%). Also, it is the highest detected after first passing the threshold (0.250 parasites/uL). Thus, it is hard to say if they would go on to be severe or not, or if there were simply more hours of replication time between infection and PCR detection between the individuals. Within the paper, parasitemia status of humans and macaques were categorically defined based on above and below the average parasitemia at time treatment was initiated. The text should more accurately reflect this by classifying groups as above average parasitemia and below average parasitemia. Additionally, none of the humans or macaques progressed to “severe malaria”, as such this phrase should not be used in the text.
c. In various places in the text (e.g., Line 42, Line 89, etc.) the authors make claims the results “strongly” associate a microbial outcome with malaria outcome. Yet, in many cases the statistical analyses are barely significant. The inclusion of “strong” should be removed in these instances.
2. The authors should provide information on the human subjects (ages, sex, nationality, HbA/S status – if known, etc.). These covariates should be accounted for in the bacterial community analyses. Additionally, the authors should provide a clear description of which subjects received placebo, KAF156 – including dosage, or Malarone. Again, these differential treatments should also be accounted for in stool samples collected post treatment to assess for any treatment induced effects. Finally, the “baseline” stool sample was indicated as being collected -2 to +2 days after infection. Analysis of whether there were differences in when the stool was collected between the severe and mild groups would be helpful to rule out whether that had any impact on microbiome differences.
a. With differential treatments and differential timing of treatments, the study may be better off focusing on association between the pre-infection stool samples and malaria outcomes.
3. Stool samples were reported to be frozen up to 24 hours post collection. As this is a considerable length of time in which bacterial communities can change quite considerably, how much variation in time to -80C is there between subjects and does this explain HC (HC1, HC2, or HC3) status?
4. Bioinformatic analyses
a. The analyses and conclusions would be strengthened by inclusion of multiple alpha diversity metrics.
b. Likewise, the authors should conduct and report on multiple beta diversity metrics.
c. It is not clear that center log ratio (CLR) transformation is the most appropriate. The authors should also report bacteria community analysis on non-transformed read counts.
d. L194: Was differential abundance done on CLR-transformed read counts? It is also not clear if raw read counts were normalized before DESeq2 analysis.
e. Have the authors used appropriate statistical tests for longitudinal analysis?

a. Bottom of Panel A indicates Study “Week”, this should be “Day”
b. L212: How many days p.i. for each participant did it take to reach 250 parasites/ml? Are there differences in time to antimalarial treatment between HC1-HC3? Time to treatment (time to peak parasite level) might be related to malaria severity. Did gut microbiota composition affect time to peak parasitemia? When was peak parasitemia reached?
c. Panel C should include CI in the graph.

How often was parasitemia measured in the subjects and can the data be presented as area under the parasitemia curve to provide a more cumulative assessment of the parasite burden within each subject over the course of the study? Differences in parasitemia are not that large, and possibly attributable to differences in time between infection and detection. Do the authors have precise time (hours) between infection and parasitemia burden surpassing the treatment threshold? Was parasitemia measured in all individuals at defined time points post infection?

### Reviewer 2

This paper examines the microbiome of (1) humans who are challenged with P. falciapurum malaria by infected mosquito bite and (2) NHP who are challenged with P.fragile malaria by injection of infected red blood cells. Both the humans and the NHP were subdivided into two groups, “high parasitemia” and “low parasitemia”. There were microbiome differences between the two groups that were identified with unsupervised clustering. My main concerns with this article are with the clinical definitions and descriptions of the CHMI.
Human CHMI:
- The human CHMI was conducted as part of an antimalarial drug study (KAF156). The current paper evaluates microbiomes from 35 participants in that study, from the placebo group, the 20 mg group, and the 50 mg group (lines 103-104. Of note, in looking at the original publication of KAF157, 3 of the volunteers in the 50 mg group did not get malaria. Therefore, their inclusion in this study is questionable.
- The participants were divided into two groups of “mild” or “severe” parasitemia (lines 218-219) based on whether their parasitemia was above or below a median parasitemia value. This is an extremely flawed way to differentiate the participants clinically. All of the participants were diagnosed with a highly sensitive molecular test. Based on the parent study, few had malaria symptoms, and none had severe malaria (if the clinical study site had allowed severe malaria to occur in the context of a drug efficacy study, this would be unethical). All mention of “severe malaria” and “severe parasitemia” needs to be removed from the manuscript if it is considered for publication. In addition, although the parasitemia levels are quantitative, the timing of sample collection in relation to the exact time of the CHMI and the exact time within the synchronized cycles of parasite emergence from RBC all affect the parasitemia levels. High parasitemia levels in the setting of ongoing malaria infection correlate with malaria severity. Differences between very low levels that are detected soon after blood stage infection has started also reflect some amount of luck (what time was the CHMI 8 days ago? What time was the volunteers appointment on the day of the PCR blood draw). This makes dividing a grouping of 35 very low parasitemias, 3 of which had a value of “ZERO” into two groups questionable.
- Nonetheless, the authors have found differences between the two groups (figure 1B) that may be worth considering. However, the statistics that differentiate the two groups of parasitemia within the three clusters (lines 220-228) are not described and need to be specified. Also, it would be helpful to know the actual parasitemia levels that were being discussed (which presumably were very low).
- Consider a discussion of the fact that most of the malaria infection was a liver infection. The blood stage of infection was brief before treatment was initiated – how does this relate to your postulations about the authors’ observations of the microbiome?
NHP challenge:
- The authors state that this is a new challenge model and provide a rationale for why this challenge model is suitable for microbiome/malaria studies. As a new model, many important details were lacking:
o What clinical manifestations were observed in the animals, and what parasitemia levels were these clinical manifestations associated with? Line 300 states that P.fragile induces similar clinical signs in RM as in Pf in humans – does this include cerebral malaria and other clinical manifestations of severe malaria? Also, which/how many of the animals needed the escalated treatment regimens, and which did not?
o Treatment regimen questions: Why did the treatment begin only after parasitema was >0.5% and not as soon as parasitemia was detectable? The treatment regimens appeared to be titrated to be lower than abortive – there was an expectation that one regimen could be given for 2 weeks consecutively without clearing parasitemia. If sub-abortive treatment was being used, why?
o How was “high parasite load” defined (line 304)? (defined for the humans but I did not see it for the RM.
o Line 349 “more severe P. fragile infection” – without information about clinical symptoms in this new animal model, I don’t know how to assess this (whereas in humans there were NO severe P. falciparum infections)
Relating the human challenge to the NHP challenge: Human challenge was by infected mosquito bite, therefore, there was 7 days of clinically silent liver infection prior to blood stage infection, which was treated at a very early stage (because it was detected molecularly, which is a very sensitive method of detection. NHP challenge was by injection of infected RBC, so there is no liver stage infection. NHP challenge seemed to be permissive of ongoing parasitemia, and it is unknown what symptoms the NHP had. The many differences between the human challenge and the NHP challenge, and whether the data are comparable to each other in consideration of all these differences need to be discussed.

### Reviewer 3

This is an interesting study but there are a few areas that require further clarification, and the overall conclusion is not clearly demonstrated by the results and figures as they currently are presented.
Abstract
- How similar is P. fragile to P. falciparum? Since these are being directly compared, the authors should explicitly compare how similar or different these two infections are
- Some statements seem over-stated, like “the combined weight of this evidence demonstrates that pre-infection GI microbiome composition is highly indicative of P. falciparum disease risk” (but yet the combined data is not on P. falciparum, half of it is on P. fragile)
Materials and Methods
- This is a nice sized human study (35 people) paired with a nice sized macaque study (16)
- Stool samples are collected in such a way that it is unclear whether there was enough time for any microbes to replicate during the time period between collection and storage (“within 24hours of collection”). A major suggestion here is that the authors need to do an analysis of time interval between collection and freezing and the results (if there is indeed an impact of time interval between collection and freezing, this would undermine the results and suggest that some of the collections were not frozen down quick enough to get a good sense of the microbial community)
- The stool collection for the macaques is well done and thought-out with respect to collecting stool from individual animals and immediately storing it at -80C
- Why do the authors use the 357F-806R primers (those published and used originally by the Earth Microbiome Project)? These are not necessarily the best primers for studies related to human gut microbiome health. I think other options should have been considered, or at least the authors should consider whether they are missing any information that they could have gained by using a different set of primers.
Results
- The authors should clarify whether the HC1 group could have another issue that confounds the data (e.g. low yield). The authors should show an analysis in which they see whether any metadata affect the groupings (e.g., total DNA yield, time between collection and freezing, etc)
- Similarly, in the rhesus macaque study, the authors should also test and consider whether there is a cage/room effect. Even though the authors do a great job of making sure they are collecting the stool from a specific animal, this doesn’t rule out the very likely possibility that socially housed animals may have more similar microbiomes than those in which they are not housed. The authors should do a analysis with metadata to see whether any of their clustering patterns are associated with these logistical factors (e.g., cage, room)
- In Line 323, I am unclear on how the authors conclude that “parasite burden was primarily driven by major compositional differences, rather than variable levels of microbiota found in both groups”. This point should be further explained. Particularly the idea that parasite burden itself is “driven” by microbiome differences. I did not find evidence in this paper that parasite burden is definitively “driven” by microbiome differences.
Discussion

- The overall idea seems to be that pre-infection microbiome composition can predict the severity of the malaria infection. Could the authors create a model to test this theory (by using part of their data and doing cross-validation to see if this holds up?)
- Going back to the main conclusion of the paper, the authors state that they “identified a high-risk microbial signature that is strongly associated with increased risk of developing severe parasitemia” and they say they find this in both humans and rhesus macaques, but after reading the paper and looking at the figures, I still am not clear on what exact microbes are associated with this increased risk of severe disease (that are in common between humans and rhesus macaques).
